     4	/-!
     5	# Generalized Pauli operators and EPR states
     6	
     7	The definitions here use finite matrix entries and rank-one projectors, so they
     8	are usable by the later game statements without introducing an abstract
     9	operator algebra.  The Fourier/orthogonality identities are retained as named
    10	proof obligations for subsequent stages.
    11	
    12	## References
    13	
    14	The source-facing nodes are `def:lin-reg`, `def:EPR`, `def:generalized-pauli`,
    15	and `lem:pauli-observable-expansion` in
    16	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:494-652`.  The paper origin is
    17	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:908-1161`.
    18	-/
    19	
    20	open scoped BigOperators Matrix ComplexOrder
    21	
    22	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    23	
    24	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    25	
    26	variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K]
    27	  [Algebra (ZMod 2) K]
    28	
    29	/-- The two generalized Pauli bases used by the test in `def:generalized-pauli`,
    30	blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
    31	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    32	-/
    33	inductive PauliKind where
    34	  | X
    35	  | Z
    36	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    37	
    38	/-- The binary character used for generalized Pauli phases; see
    39	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1081`.
    40	
    41	It is public because the Fourier expansion declarations below expose this
    42	character in their statement types. -/
    43	noncomputable def phaseSign (t : ZMod 2) : ℂ :=
    44	  if t = 0 then 1 else -1
    45	
    46	/--
    47	The shift operator `τ^X(a)`.  Blueprint `def:generalized-pauli`,
    48	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`; paper origin
    49	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    50	-/
    51	noncomputable def tauShift (a : K) : Op K :=
    52	  fun i j => if i = j + a then 1 else 0
    53	
    54	/--
    55	The phase operator `τ^Z(b)`, with the fixed binary trace in the phase.  It is
    56	the second operator of `def:generalized-pauli` (blueprint lines 529-571; paper
    57	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`).
    58	-/
    59	noncomputable def tauPhase (b : K) : Op K :=
    60	  fun i j => if i = j then phaseSign (binTrace K (b * j)) else 0
    61	
    62	/-- The single-qudit eigenvector coordinate used in the tensor-product basis;
    63	see `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1126-1161`. -/
    64	private noncomputable def singlePauliVec (W : PauliKind) (e x : K) : ℂ :=
    65	  match W with
    66	  | .Z => if x = e then 1 else 0
    67	  | .X =>
    68	      (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card K : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ * phaseSign (binTrace K (e * x))
    69	
    70	/--
    71	The normalized single/multi-qudit eigenvector for a Pauli basis label.  For an
    72	index type `ι`, the input `e : ι → K` labels the tensor-product basis vector.
    73	This is the vector form of `def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint
    74	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:550-570`, paper origin
    75	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1101-1122`.
    76	-/
    77	noncomputable def pauliVec {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    78	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) (x : ι → K) : ℂ :=
    79	  ∏ i : ι, singlePauliVec W (e i) (x i)
    80	
    81	/--
    82	The rank-one projector onto `pauliVec W e`.  This is the projective measurement
    83	element `τ^W_e` in `def:generalized-pauli` (blueprint lines 562-570; paper
    84	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1101-1122`).
    85	-/
    86	noncomputable def pauliProj {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    87	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) : Op (ι → K) :=
    88	  Matrix.vecMulVec (pauliVec W e) (fun x => star (pauliVec W e x))
    89	
    90	/-- A compact operator-valued form of a generalized Pauli observable from
    91	`def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
    92	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    93	-/
    94	noncomputable def tauObservable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    95	    (W : PauliKind) (a : ι → K) : Op (ι → K) :=
    96	  fun x y =>
    97	    ∏ i : ι,
    98	      match W with
    99	      | .X => tauShift (a i) (x i) (y i)
   100	      | .Z => tauPhase (a i) (x i) (y i)
   101	
   102	/--
   103	The EPR vector on a finite label space.  Blueprint `def:EPR`,
   104	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:513-523`; paper origin
   105	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`.
   106	-/
   107	noncomputable def eprState (V : Type*) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
   108	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (V × V) :=
   109	  (EuclideanSpace.equiv (V × V) ℂ).symm
   110	    (fun p : V × V =>
   111	      if p.1 = p.2 then (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card V : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ else 0)
   112	
   113	/-- The EPR vector is normalized on a nonempty finite carrier; see
   114	`def:EPR`, `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`. -/
   115	theorem eprState_norm (V : Type*) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
   116	    ‖eprState V‖ = 1 := by
   117	  sorry
   118	
   119	/--
   120	Fourier expansion of a generalized Pauli observable in the Pauli projectors.
   121	This is `lem:pauli-observable-expansion`, equations `eq:pauli-obs-proj` and
   122	`eq:pauli-inversion-0`, in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:638-652`;
   123	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1141-1161`.
   124	Both directions are deliberately left as proof-level obligations in stage 4.1.
   125	-/
   126	theorem tauObservable_eq_sum_pauliProj {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   127	    (W : PauliKind) (a : ι → K) :
   128	    tauObservable W a =
   129	      ∑ e : ι → K, phaseSign (binTrace K (dotProduct a e)) • pauliProj W e := by
   130	  sorry
   131	
   132	/-- The inverse Fourier expansion of a Pauli projector
   133	(`lem:pauli-observable-expansion`), blueprint
   134	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:638-652`, paper origin
   135	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1141-1161`.
   136	-/
   137	theorem pauliProj_eq_avg_tauObservable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   138	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) :
   139	    pauliProj W e =
   140	      (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ)⁻¹ •
   141	        ∑ a : ι → K, phaseSign (binTrace K (dotProduct a e)) • tauObservable W a := by
   142	  sorry
   143	
   144	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

    29	/--
    30	A fixed finite-field model records the carrier and the chosen coding of its
    31	elements by `Fin q`.  The algebra structure and stored basis data make explicit
    32	the paper's once-and-for-all self-dual normal-basis convention; they are
    33	deliberately part of the model rather than quantified afresh by the soundness

    35	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`, paper origin
    36	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:653-728`.

    40	structure FixedFieldModel (q : ℕ) extends MIPStarRE.LDT.FieldModel.{0} q where

    43	  /-- Dimension of the chosen basis over the prime subfield. -/
    44	  basisDim : ℕ
    45	  /-- The chosen basis dimension is odd, as required for a self-dual normal basis
    46	  over the binary field. -/
    47	  basisDimOdd : Odd basisDim
    48	  /-- The admissible field-size relation for the chosen basis dimension. -/
    49	  basisCard : q = 2 ^ basisDim
    50	  /-- The chosen basis of `K` over `ZMod 2`. -/
    51	  basis : Module.Basis (Fin basisDim) (ZMod 2) K
    52	  /--
    53	  The inherited coding of `K` is the natural binary encoding of the stored
    54	  basis coordinates.  This field records the source's `downsize` convention
    55	  rather than allowing an unrelated permutation of `Fin q`.  It is the
    56	  coordinate clause of `def:binary-representation` in
    57	  `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`, with paper origin
    58	  `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:669-680`.
    59	  -/
    60	  representation_natural :
    61	    ∀ v : Fin basisDim → ZMod 2,
    62	      (toFieldModel.equiv (basis.equivFun.symm v)).val =
    63	        ∑ i : Fin basisDim, if v i = 1 then 2 ^ i.1 else 0
    64	  /-- Self-duality of the chosen basis with respect to the field trace. -/
    65	  selfDual : ∀ i j, Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K (basis i * basis j) =
    66	    if i = j then 1 else 0
    67	  /-- Normality of the chosen basis, recorded by a Frobenius generator. -/
    68	  normal : ∃ α : K, ∀ i, basis i = α ^ (2 ^ i.1)

450		\downsize_q (a + b) = \downsize_q(a) + \downsize_q(b)\;.
   451	\end{equation*}
   452	Second, multiplication by a field element in $\F_{q^k}$ corresponds to a linear
   453	map on $\F_{q}^k$.
   454	For all $a \in \F_{q^k}$, there exists a matrix $K_a \in \Matrix_k (\Fq)$ such
   455	that for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   456	\begin{equation*}
   457		\downsize_q (a b) = K_a \, \downsize_q(b)\;.
   458	\end{equation*}
   459	The matrix $K_a$ is called the \emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to
   460	  basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$}.
   461	
   462	We extend the map $\downsize_q$ to vectors, matrices and sets over $\F_{q^k}$.
   463	For $v = (v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$, define
   464	\begin{equation*}
   465	  \downsize_q (v) = \bigl( \downsize_q (v_i) \bigr)_{i=1}^n \in \Fq^{kn}\;.
   466	\end{equation*}
   467	Similarly, for matrix $M = (M_{i, j}) \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$, define
   468	\begin{equation*}
   469	  \downsizem_q (M) = \bigl( K_{M_{i, j}} \bigr) \in \Matrix_{mk, nk} (\Fq)\;,
   470	\end{equation*}
   471	the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th block is the multiplication table $K_{M_{i,
   472	    j}}$ of $M_{i, j}$ with respect to basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$.
   473	For a set $S$ of vectors in $\F_{q^k}^n$, define
   474	\begin{equation*}
   475		\downsize_q(S) = \{ \downsize_q(v) : v \in S \}\;.
   476	\end{equation*}
   477	We omit the subscript and write $\downsize$ and $\downsizem$ for $\downsize_q$
   478	and $\downsizem_q$ respectively when $q$ equals to $p$, the characteristic of
   479	the field.
   480	
   481	The \emph{trace of\/ $\F_{q^k}$ over\/ $\Fq$} is defined as
   482	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   483	  \tr_{q^k \to q} :\; a \,\mapsto \, \Tr(K_a)
   484	\end{equation}
   485	for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $\Tr(K_a)$ is the trace of the multiplication table
   486	of $a$ with respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$.
   487	By definition, the trace is an $\Fq$-linear map from $\F_{q^k}$ to
   488	$\Fq$. The trace is in fact independent of the choice of basis, which
   489	can be seen from the following equivalent definition~\cite[Definition 2.1.80]{mullen2013handbook}:
   490	\[
   491		\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j = 0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   492	\]
   493	
   494	A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', e_2', \ldots, e_k' \}$ of $\{e_1, e_2, \ldots,
   495	e_k\}$ is a basis such that $\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for
   496	all $i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$.
   497	A \emph{self-dual basis} is one that is equal to its dual.
   498	If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set $\{ \alpha^{q^j} \}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a
   499	basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\Fq$, the basis is called a \emph{normal
   500	  basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not exist for all fields but are guaranteed to exist under
   501	certain conditions; in particular, if $q = 2$ and $k$ is odd, as will
   502	be shown in \Cref{lem:efficient_basis}.
   503	
   504	We record some convenient facts about the maps $\downsize(\cdot)$ and
   505	$\downsizem(\cdot)$ for self-dual bases.
   506	
   507	\begin{lemma}
   508	  \label{lem:downsize_field}
   509	  Let $q$ be a prime power, $k$ an integer and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual basis for
   510	  $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.
   511	  The map $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ corresponding to $\{e_i\}$ satisfies the
   512	  following properties:
   513	  \begin{enumerate}
   514	  \item For all $x \in \F_{q^k}$, $\downsize_q(x) = \bigl( \tr_{q^k \to
   515	      q}(xe_1),\ldots,\tr_{q^k \to q}(xe_k) \bigr)$.
   516	  \item For all $x,y \in \F_{q^k}$, $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \downsize_q(x) \cdot
   517	    \downsize_q(y)$.
   518	  \item For all $M \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in
   519	    \F_{q^k}^n$, we have $\downsizem_q(M) \downsize_q(v) = \downsize_q(Mv)$.
   520	  \end{enumerate}
   521	\end{lemma}
   522	 
   523	\begin{proof}
   524	  We show each property by direct calculation.
   525	  \begin{enumerate}
   526	    \item Let $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$. Then by the definition of
   527	    $\downsize_q$, $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$. Multiplying both sides by $e_j$
   528	    and taking the trace yields $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i
   529	    \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j) = x_j$, where the last equality is by
   530	    self-duality of the basis.
   531	    \item Write $\downsize_q(x) = (x_1, \dots, x_k)$ and $\downsize_q(y) =
   532	      (y_1, \dots, y_k)$. Then
   533	      \begin{align*}
   534	        \tr_{q^k \to q} (xy) &= \tr_{q^k \to q}(\sum_{ij} x_i y_j e_i
   535	                               e_j) \\
   536	                             &= \sum_{ij} x_i y_j \tr_{q^k \to q}(  e_i
   537	                               e_j) \\
   538	                             &= \downsize_q(x) \cdot \downsize_q(y),
   539	      \end{align*}
   540	      where the last equality uses the self-duality of the basis.
   541	    \item
   542	      We compute the $i$th $\F_q^k$-block of $\downsize_q(Mv)$:
   543	      \begin{align*}
   544	        \downsize_q(Mv)_i &= \sum_{ij} \downsize_q(M_{ij} v_j) \\
   545	                          &= \sum_{ij} K_{M_{ij}} \downsize_q(v_j) \\
   546	                          &= \downsizem_q(M)_{ij} \downsize_q(v_j) ,
   547	      \end{align*}
   548	      where we have applied the definition of the multiplication table
   549	      $K_{M_{ij}}$ and the map $\downsizem_q(\cdot)$.
   550	  \end{enumerate}
   551	\end{proof}

   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =
   747	    \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} b^{2^i} = \tr(b)\;,
   748	  \]
   749	  where we use that $b^{2^k} = b$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.
   751	  It cannot be the case that $\tr(e_i) = 0$ for all $i$.
   752	  Suppose that this were the case.
   753	  This would imply that $\tr(b) = 0$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   754	  But then for all $j \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$ and for some $b \neq 0$, we would
   755	  also have by item 1 of \Cref{lem:downsize_field} that $b_j = \tr(b e_j) = 0$ where $b = \sum_j b_j e_j$ with $b_j \in
   756	  \F_2$.
   757	  This implies that $b$ is the all zero element of $\F_{2^k}$, which is a
   758	  contradiction.
   759	  Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i=1, 2, \ldots, k$.
   760	
   761		The ``furthermore'' part follows item 1 of
   762	        \Cref{lem:downsize_field}:
   763	        \begin{equation*}
   764	          \downsize(1) = (\tr(1 \cdot e_1), \dots, \tr(1 \cdot e_k))
   765	          = (1, \dots, 1).
   766	        \end{equation*}
   767	\end{proof}

   192		Let $q$ be a prime power and $k \ge 1$ an integer, so that $\F_q$ is a

   271			\item for all $x, y \in \F_{q^k}$,
   272			      $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \kappa_q(x) \cdot \kappa_q(y)$;

    30	\section{Key theorem forms}
    31	Let $K$ be a finite extension of $\mathbb F_p$, let
    32	$\chi(x)=\exp(2\pi i\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb F_p}(x)/p)$, and let
    33	$a,a',b\in K^n$.  The relevant identities are
    34	\[
    35	 \tau^W(a)\tau^W(a')=\tau^W(a+a'),\qquad
    36	 \tau^W(a)^p=I,
    37	\]
    38	and
    39	\[
    40	 \tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)=\chi(-a\mathbin{\cdot}b)
    41	 \tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a).
    42	\]
    43	The explicit shift and phase matrices are unitary. The second identity implies
    44	that every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $\tau^W(a)$ satisfies $\lambda^p=1$. If
    45	$V\leq K^n$ and $v\notin V^\perp$, Fourier cancellation takes the form
    46	\[
    47	 \mathbb E_{u\in V}\chi(u\mathbin{\cdot}v)=0.
    48	\]

    50	\section{Source and formal scope}
    51	The source defines the shift and phase matrices and states their product,
    52	$p$-th-power, unitarity, spectral, and twisted-commutation properties in
    53	\cite[lines 1056--1095]{Ji2020MIPStar}. It uses the same character for Fourier
    54	cancellation over a subspace at lines 1124--1132 and extends the twisted
    55	relation to several qudits at lines 1141--1150. These assertions depend on the
    56	characteristic $p$; they are not intrinsically binary.
    57	
    58	The formal definitions \path{primeTauShift}, \path{primeTauPhase}, and
    59	\path{primeTauObservable} use the canonical character \path{ffChar} in
    60	characteristic $p$.  Their theorem statements cover the identities above for
    61	arbitrary $p$.  The declarations whose names begin with
    62	\path{tauObservable} or use \path{phaseSign} instead specialize to
    63	$p=2$, where $\chi(x)=(-1)^{\operatorname{Tr}(x)}$.  This specialization is
    64	appropriate only for the subsequent test, whose admissible sizes satisfy
    65	$q=2^k$; it is not substituted for the general statements.
    66	
    67	The proofs can be obtained directly from the displayed matrices.  A shift is a
    68	permutation matrix, a phase matrix has diagonal entries of modulus one, and a
    69	tensor product of such matrices is unitary.  Iterating the product identity

    72	$v\notin V^\perp$, the map $u\mapsto\chi(u\cdot v)$ is a nontrivial character

    44	\section{Key theorem forms}
    45	
    46	Three statements must be kept apart.  Throughout, $\game$ denotes a symmetric
    47	two-player one-round game and $\eps \ge 0$ a real parameter; the notation is
    48	introduced in the next section.

    50	\begin{enumerate}
    51	  \item \textbf{Source form (attainment form).}  If
    52	  $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$, then there exists a symmetric and projective
    53	  strategy $\strategy$ with $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps$.
    54	  \item \textbf{Approximate form (what the source proof establishes).}  If
    55	  $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$, then for every $\eps' > \eps$ there exists a
    56	  symmetric and projective strategy $\strategy$ with
    57	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps'$.
    58	  \item \textbf{Given-strategy form (value-preserving symmetrization).}  If
    59	  $\strategy'$ is any strategy for $\game$ with
    60	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps$, then there exists a symmetric and
    61	  projective strategy $\strategy$ with
    62	  $\val^*(\game, \strategy) = \val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps$.
    63	\end{enumerate}

    66	strategy supplied by the definition of the supremum; this yields the second

    69	the lemma, in the source and in this project, consumes only the second or the

    72	\section{The source assertion}
    73	
    74	A two-player one-round game
    75	$\game = (\mathcal X, \mathcal A, \mu, D)$ in compact symmetric notation
    76	consists of a finite question alphabet $\mathcal X$, a finite answer alphabet
    77	$\mathcal A$, a symmetric question distribution $\mu$ on
    78	$\mathcal X \times \mathcal X$, and a decision predicate $D$ treating the two
    79	players symmetrically.  A tensor product strategy
    80	$\strategy = (\ket\psi, A, B)$ consists of a unit vector $\ket\psi$ in a
    81	tensor product $\mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ of \emph{finite-dimensional}
    82	Hilbert spaces together with POVMs $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ for the two
    83	players; its value $\val^*(\game, \strategy)$ is the acceptance probability,
    84	and the value of the game is the supremum
    85	\begin{equation*}
    86	  \val^*(\game) = \sup_{\strategy} \val^*(\game, \strategy)
    87	\end{equation*}
    88	over all tensor product strategies.  A strategy is projective if all its
    89	measurements are projective, and symmetric if the state is
    90	permutation-invariant on $\mathcal H \ot \mathcal H$ and both players use the
    91	same measurements.
    92	
    93	The symmetrization lemma of \cite[Section~5]{Ji2020MIPStar} asserts:%
    94	\footnote{The statement is at
    95	\path{references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex}, lines~94--99,
    96	and its proof at lines~101--132.  The blueprint statement restored to this form
    97	is \path{lem:symmetric-strat} in
    98	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex}.}
    99	if $\game$ is a symmetric game with $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$ for some
   100	$\eps \ge 0$, then
   101	\begin{equation*}
   102	  \exists\, \strategy = (\ket{\psi}, M) \text{ symmetric and projective}
   103	  \quad\text{with}\quad
   104	  \val^*(\game, \strategy) \ge 1-\eps.
   105	  \tag{\path{lem:symmetric-strat}}
   106	\end{equation*}
   107	
   108	Its proof runs as follows.  For every $\eps' > \eps$ the definition of the
   109	supremum supplies a strategy $\strategy' = (\ket{\psi'}, A, B)$ with
   110	$\val^*(\game, \strategy') \ge 1-\eps'$.  By Naimark dilation in the completed
   111	projective form of \cite[Theorem~5.1]{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} one may take
   112	$\ket{\psi'} \in \C^d_{A'} \ot \C^d_{B'}$ for some integer $d$ with all
   113	measurements projective.  One then forms the permutation-invariant state
   114	\begin{equation*}
   115	  \ket{\psi} = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt 2}
   116	  \bigl( \ket{0}_A \ket{1}_B \ket{\psi'}_{A'B'}
   117	       + \ket{1}_A \ket{0}_B \ket{\psi'_\tau}_{A'B'} \bigr)
   118	\end{equation*}
   119	on $(\C^2 \ot \C^d) \ot (\C^2 \ot \C^d)$, where $\ket{\psi'_\tau}$ permutes
   120	the two players' registers, and the block-diagonal projective measurements
   121	$M^x_a = \ket{0}\!\bra{0} \ot A^x_a + \ket{1}\!\bra{1} \ot B^x_a$.  Symmetry
   122	of $D$ gives $\val^*(\game, (\ket\psi, M)) = \val^*(\game, \strategy')$.  The
   123	construction is therefore \emph{value-preserving}: applied to any strategy it
   124	produces a symmetric projective strategy of exactly the same value.  What the
   125	proof establishes is thus the given-strategy form, hence the approximate form;
   126	the printed conclusion is the attainment form.
   127	
   128	\section{Why attainment does not follow}
   129	
   130	The supremum defining $\val^*(\game)$ ranges over strategies on
   131	finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces of unbounded dimension.  The strategies
   132	$\strategy'_{\eps'}$ produced for $\eps' \downarrow \eps$ may require
   133	dimensions $d(\eps')$ growing without bound, and there is no compactness
   134	across dimensions from which a limiting finite-dimensional strategy of value
   135	at least $1-\eps$ could be extracted.  A symmetric projective strategy of
   136	value at least $1-\eps = \val^*(\game)$ would attain the supremum, so the
   137	printed conclusion is equivalent, under its hypothesis, to the assertion that
   138	$\val^*(\game)$ is attained by some strategy.  No general principle supplies
   139	this: it is known, and recalled in the introduction of the source itself, that
   140	the set of finite-dimensional quantum correlations is not closed and differs
   141	from the set of infinite-dimensional spatial correlations, so limits of
   142	finite-dimensional strategies need not be realized by any finite-dimensional
   143	strategy.  Whether some symmetric game realizes the failure --- a game whose
   144	value is attained by no tensor product strategy, presented together with the
   145	exposing functional as a decision predicate --- is a separate question that
   146	this note does not need to settle.  The local verdict is about the proof: the
   147	cited argument proves the approximate form and does not prove the attainment
   148	form.
   149	
   150	\section{Uses of the lemma}
   151	
   152	The source invokes the lemma twice.
   153	
   154	First, in the soundness proof for the oracularization transformation, the
   155	argument fixes a strategy $\strategy^{\mathrm{orac}}$ for the oracularized game
   156	``with value $1-\eps$'' and applies the lemma to assume without loss of
   157	generality that it is projective.%
   158	\footnote{\path{references/qpbt-paper/10_oracularization.tex},
   159	lines~317--321.}
   160	Here the input is a given strategy, not the value of the game; the
   161	given-strategy form applies verbatim and preserves the value exactly, so the
   162	use is justified by what the proof establishes.
   163	
   164	Second, in the soundness proof for answer reduction, the argument assumes the
   165	strict inequality $\val^*(\game) > 1-\eps$ and concludes that there is a
   166	symmetric projective strategy of value greater than $1-\eps$.%
   167	\footnote{\path{references/qpbt-paper/11_answer_reduction.tex},
   168	lines~2322--2332.}
   169	Writing $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps_0$ with $\eps_0 < \eps$ and applying the
   170	approximate form with $\eps' = (\eps+\eps_0)/2$ produces a symmetric
   171	projective strategy of value at least $1-\eps' > 1-\eps$.  A strict lower
   172	bound on the supremum thus passes through the approximate form; attainment is
   173	not used.
   174	
   175	In this project, the soundness statements of the Pauli basis test track
   176	quantify over strategies assumed to succeed with probability at least
   177	$1-\eps$, so any symmetrization step starts from a given strategy and consumes
   178	the given-strategy form.  The blueprint currently records the lemma as part of
   179	the games vocabulary and has no downstream dependency on it; the two source
   180	uses above belong to transformations outside the scope of the present
   181	development.  Consequently, no consumer of the lemma --- in the source or here
   182	--- requires the attainment form.
   183	
   184	\section{Comparison with the blueprint}
   185	
   186	The blueprint \cite{MIPStarREBlueprint} states the lemma in the source shape.
   187	Its proof records the value-preserving construction and the approximate form
   188	that the construction yields, and explicitly marks the remaining attainment
   189	step as unproved, citing this note; an accompanying remark summarizes the
   190	obstruction.  An earlier revision of the blueprint had instead weakened the
   191	source-labelled conclusion to the approximate form; following the project's
   192	proof-gap protocol, the source-labelled statement is restored and the missing
   193	step is tracked in the proof rather than absorbed into the statement. The
   194	source-shaped declaration \leanid{exists\_symmetric\_projective\_strategy} is
   195	now linked to the lemma; its proof remains the tracked attainment obligation.
   196	
   197	\section{Conclusion}
   198	
   199	The verdict is a proof-level gap in the cited lemma: the symmetrization
   200	argument proves the given-strategy and approximate forms, while the printed
   201	conclusion additionally asserts that the supremum defining $\val^*(\game)$ is
   202	attained, which does not follow.  The gap is harmless for the results built on
   203	the lemma, since both uses in the source, and all planned uses in this
   204	project, proceed from a given strategy of value at least $1-\eps$ or from a
   205	strict lower bound on the value, for which the value-preserving construction
   206	suffices.  For stage~4 (formalization) the recommendation is: formalize the
   207	given-strategy symmetrization lemma as the workhorse statement; keep the
   208	source-labelled lemma in source shape with the attainment step an explicit,
   209	tracked proof obligation; and do not strengthen the source-labelled statement's
   210	hypotheses or weaken its conclusion silently.  If a later investigation
   211	settles the counterexample question for symmetric games, the statement should
   212	then be reclassified from an unproved step to a documented statement
   213	correction.

    36	\section{Key theorem forms}
    37	
    38	Let $a\geq 1$ and $0<b<1$ be the universal constants in the soundness
    39	function
    40	\[
    41	  \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q)
    42	    = a(md)^a\bigl(\eps^b+q^{-b}+2^{-bmd}\bigr).
    43	\]
    44	For $R\geq4$, let $c$ be the least even integer at least $(a+b)/b$, set
    45	$k=c\lceil\log_2\log_2 R\rceil+1$ and $q=2^k$, and let $j$ be determined by
    46	$2^j\leq c\lceil\log_2 R\rceil+1<2^{j+1}$. The remaining canonical parameters
    47	are $m=2^j$ and $d=1$. In particular,
    48	$m\geq (c/2)\log_2 R\geq\log_2 R$. The required estimate for the third summand is
    49	\[
    50	  a m^a 2^{-bm} \leq C'(\log R)^{-b},
    51	\]
    52	for a constant $C'$ depending only on $a$ and $b$.  This estimate, together
    53	with the source bounds for the first two summands, gives the asserted
    54	polylogarithmic bound for $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}$.
    55	
    56	\section{The source comparison}
    57	
    58	The canonical parameters are defined in \cite[lines~1503--1514]{Ji2020MIPStar},
    59	and the bound and its proof occupy lines~1520--1562. At line~1543 the proof
    60	replaces $2^{-bmd}$ by $q^{-b}$ using the assertion $k\leq m$.%
    61	\footnote{Tracked in
    62	\href{https://github.com/Dengnifer/MIPStarRE-A/issues/16}{GitHub issue \#16}.
    63	The canonical parameter definition is at
    64	\path{references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex},
    65	lines~1503--1514; the bound and its proof are at lines~1520--1562, with the
    66	disputed comparison at line~1543.}
    67	That comparison does not follow from the stated parameter choice.  For example,
    68	the allowed values $a=1$ and $b=1/2$ give $c=4$, and $R=5$ gives $k=9$ but
    69	$m=8$.  Thus the displayed justification is false even though the lemma's
    70	conclusion remains valid.
    71	
    72	The third term can instead be bounded independently of $q$.  Since $d=1$ and
    73	$m\geq (c/2)\log R\geq\log R$,
    74	\[
    75	  2^{-bm}\leq R^{-b}.
    76	\]
    77	The accompanying upper bound $m\leq 2c\log R$ therefore gives
    78	\[
    79	  a m^a2^{-bm}
    80	    \leq a(2c)^a(\log R)^aR^{-b}
    81	    = a(2c)^a\bigl((\log R)^{a+b}R^{-b}\bigr)(\log R)^{-b}.
    82	\]
    83	The parenthesized factor is bounded on $R\geq4$: it is continuous and tends
    84	to zero as $R$ tends to infinity.  Absorbing its supremum into the universal
    85	constant yields the required estimate.

   241	\begin{definition}
   242	  Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_i\}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$.
   243	  For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$, $v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V$,
   244	  define the \emph{dot product}
   245	  \begin{equation*}
   246	    u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
   247	  \end{equation*}
   248	  Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. The \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
   249	  \begin{equation*}
   250	    S^\perp \,=\, \big\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0
   251	    \text{ for all }  v \in S \big\}\;.
   252	  \end{equation*}
   253	  Although the notation $S^\perp$ does not explicitly refer to $V$, the ambient
   254	  space will always be clear from context.
   255	\end{definition}
   256	
   257	We note that over finite fields, the notion of orthogonality does not possess
   258	all of the same intuitive properties of orthogonality over fields such as $\R$
   259	or $\C$; for example, a non-zero subspace $S$ may be orthogonal to itself (e.g.\
   260	$\mathrm{span} \{ (1,1) \}$ over $\F_2$).
   261	However, the following remains true over all fields.
   262	
   263	\begin{lemma}
   264	  \label{lem:perp_perp}
   265	  Suppose $S$ is a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) =
   266	  \dim(V)$, and 
   267	  \begin{equation*}
   268	    (S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
   269	  \end{equation*}
   270	\end{lemma}
   271	
   272	\begin{proof}
   273	  The statement about the dimensions follows from the fact that vectors in $S^\perp$ are
   274	  the solution to a feasible linear system of equations with $\dim(S)$ linearly
   275	  independent rows; this implies that the solution space has dimension exactly
   276	  $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$.
   277	  Next, we argue that $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   278	  Let $u \in S$.
   279	  Since all vectors $v \in S^\perp$ are orthogonal to every vector in $S$,
   280	  in particular $u$, this implies that $u \in (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   281	  By dimension counting, it follows that $(S^\perp)^\perp = S$.
   282	\end{proof}

   284	\begin{definition}\label{def:complementary}
   285	  Given a linear space $V$, two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of $V$ are said to form a
   286	  pair of \emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
   287	\begin{equation*}
   288	  S \cap T = \{ 0 \}, \quad S + T = V\;.
   289	\end{equation*}
   290	In this case, we write $V = S \oplus T$.
   291	Any $x\in V$ can be written as $x = x^S + x^T$ for $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$
   292	in a unique way.
   293	We refer to $x^S$ (resp.~$x^T$) as the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel
   294	  to $T$} (resp.~\emph{onto $T$ parallel to $S$}).
   295	We call the unique linear map $L: V \to V$ that maps $x \mapsto x^S$ the
   296	\emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
   297	\end{definition}
   298	
   299	A given subspace may have many different complementary subspaces: consider the
   300	example of $S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1) \}$ in $\F_2^2$.
   301	Different complementary subspaces include $T = \mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and
   302	$T' = \mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$.
   303	It is convenient to define the notion of a \emph{canonical complement} of a
   304	subspace $S$, given a basis for $S$.
   305	
   306	\begin{definition}
   307	  \label{def:canonical-complement}
   308	  Let $E$ be the standard basis of linear space $V = \F^n$.
   309	  Let $F = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly
   310	  independent vectors in $V$.
   311	  The \emph{canonical complement $F^\perp$ of $F$} is the set of $n-m$ independent
   312	  vectors defined as follows.
   313	  Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i, j}\, \hat{e}_j$.
   314		Using a canonical algorithm for Gaussian elimination that works over arbitrary
   315	  fields, transform the $m\times n$ matrix $(a_{i, j})$ to reduced row echelon
   316	  form $(b_{i, j})$.
   317	  Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices of the leading $1$ entry in each row
   318	  of $(b_{i, j})$.
   319	  The canonical complement is defined as $F^\perp = \{ \hat{e}_j : j \not\in J \}$.
   320	\end{definition}
   321	
   322	
   323	\begin{remark}
   324	We emphasize that the canonical complement $F^\perp$ is a \emph{set} (rather than
   325	a subspace), and it is defined with respect to a \emph{set} of linearly
   326	independent vectors $F$. While there are equivalent ways of defining
   327	a canonical complement of a \emph{subspace} in a basis-independent manner, 
   328	we use this particular definition because it makes it clear that
   329	the canonical complement of a set $F$ is efficiently computable. 
   330	\end{remark}
   331	
   332	\begin{remark}
   333	  Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V$.
   334	  Suppose subspace $S$ is a register subspace of $V$ spanned by
   335	  $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$.
   336	  Then it is not hard to verify that the canonical complement of $\hat{E}_{0}$ is
   337	  $\hat{E}\setminus \hat{E}_0$ and the span of the canonical complement coincides with
   338	  $S^\perp$.
   339	\end{remark}

   342	\begin{lemma}
   343	  \label{lem:canonical-complement}
   344	  Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors $F = \{v_1,\ldots,v_m \}
   345	  \subseteq V$ and let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$ as defined
   346	  in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   347	  Let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   348	  Then
   349	  \begin{equation*}
   350	   \qquad S + T = V\;,  S \cap T = \{ 0 \} \;.
   351	  \end{equation*}
   352	\end{lemma}
   353	
   354	\begin{proof}
   355	To show the first item, we must show that every vector in $V$ can be
   356	written as a sum of an element of $S$ and an element of $T$. To do
   357	this, let $A = (a_{i, j})$ be the $m\times n$ matrix over $\F$ whose
   358	rows are the vectors $v_i$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   359	  Write $A = U B$ where $U$ is invertible and $B$ is in reduced row echelon
   360	  form.
   361	  Let $J$ be the set of column indices of the leading 1 entries in
   362	  $B$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.  
   363	  Now, the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span the subpsace $S$, and the restriction of
   364	  these rows to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   365	  span $\F^m$. Thus, for any vector $u \in V$, there is some linear
   366	  combination $v$ of rows of $B$ such that $u$ and $v$ agree
   367	  restricted to the columns in $J$. In other words, there exists $v
   368	  \in S$ such that $u_j = v_j$ for all $j \in J$. Hence, $u = v + w$
   369	  for $w \in T$, where $T$ is the canonical complement.
   370	  This shows $S + T = V$.
   371	  Counting dimensions shows that necessarily $S\cap T =
   372	  \{0\}$.
   373	\end{proof}

   375	\begin{definition}
   376	  \label{def:cl-canonical}
   377	  Let $F \subseteq V$ be a set of linearly independent vectors.
   378	  Let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$.
   379	  Define the \emph{canonical linear map $L \in \End(V)$ with kernel basis $F$}
   380	  as the projector onto $T$ parallel to $S$, where $S = \mathrm{span}(F)$ and $T
   381	  = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   382	  When the basis $F$ for $S$ is clear from context, we refer to this map as the
   383	  \emph{canonical linear map with kernel $S$.}
   384	\end{definition}

   386	\begin{definition}
   387	  \label{def:Lperp}
   388	  Let $L \in \End(V)$ be a linear map, and let $F$ be a basis for
   389	  $\ker(L)^\perp$.
   390	  Define $L^\perp : V \rightarrow V$ as the canonical linear map with kernel
   391	  basis $F$.
   392	\end{definition}

   394	\begin{lemma}
   395	  \label{lem:L_perp_perp}
   396	  Let $L \in \End(V)$ be a linear map and $F$ a basis for $\ker(L)^\perp$.
   397	  Let $L^\perp \in \End(V)$ be the linear map defined in
   398	  Definition~\ref{def:Lperp}.
   399	  Then $\ker(L^\perp) = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   400	\end{lemma}

   402	\begin{proof}
   403	  First, to set notation, let $S = \mathrm{span}(F) = \ker(L)^\perp$ and $T =
   404	  \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement},
   405	  any vector $v \in V$ can be uniquely decomposed as $v = v^S +
   406	  v^T$. 
   407	
   408	  Now we will show the lemma.  First we show that if $\ker(L^\perp) \subseteq \ker(L)^\perp$. Let
   409	  $v \in \ker(L^\perp)$, and write $v = v^S + v^T$.  By the definition
   410	  of $L^\perp$, it follows that $v^T = 0$, and hence $v \in S = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   411	
   412	  It remains to show the other direction, that is $\ker(L)^\perp \subseteq
   413	  \ker(L^\perp)$. Let $v \in \ker(L)^\perp = S$. Then $v = v^S + v^T$
   414	  where $v^T = 0$, and hence by the definition of $L^\perp$, $L^\perp
   415	  v = 0$. Hence $v \in \ker(L^\perp)$.
   416	
   417	  
   418	\end{proof}

    49	\[

+\documentclass[11pt]{article}
+\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb}

+\title{Prime-Characteristic and Binary Pauli Observables}
+\author{}
+\date{2026-09-02}
+
+\begin{document}
+\maketitle
+\section{At a glance}
+\begin{itemize}
+  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source-facing statements must retain
+  arbitrary prime characteristic while the later Pauli basis test uses a
+  separately named characteristic-two specialization.
+  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} The remaining proofs should occupy one
+  algebra file of roughly 100--200 lines.
+  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Mathlib supplies finite matrix algebra
+  and finite-field facts; the generalized Pauli definitions and their
+  characteristic-two specialization are project-local.
+  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Unitarity of shift and phase
+  matrices, the $p$-th-power identity, and additive-character orthogonality.
+  The scope correction is tracked in
+  \href{https://github.com/Dengnifer/MIPStarRE-A/issues/16}{GitHub issue \#16}
+  and descends from \localissue{0002}.
+\end{itemize}
+
+\section{Key theorem forms}
+Let $K$ be a finite extension of $\mathbb F_p$, let
+$\chi(x)=\exp(2\pi i\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb F_p}(x)/p)$, and let
+$a,a',b\in K^n$.  The relevant identities are
+\[
+ \tau^W(a)\tau^W(a')=\tau^W(a+a'),\qquad
+ \tau^W(a)^p=I,
+\]
+and
+\[
+ \tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)=\chi(-a\mathbin{\cdot}b)
+ \tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a).
+\]
+The explicit shift and phase matrices are unitary. The second identity implies
+that every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $\tau^W(a)$ satisfies $\lambda^p=1$. If
+$V\leq K^n$ and $v\notin V^\perp$, Fourier cancellation takes the form
+\[
+ \mathbb E_{u\in V}\chi(u\mathbin{\cdot}v)=0.
+\]
+
+\section{Source and formal scope}
+The source defines the shift and phase matrices and states their product,
+$p$-th-power, unitarity, spectral, and twisted-commutation properties in
+\cite[lines 1056--1095]{Ji2020MIPStar}. It uses the same character for Fourier
+cancellation over a subspace at lines 1124--1132 and extends the twisted
+relation to several qudits at lines 1141--1150. These assertions depend on the
+characteristic $p$; they are not intrinsically binary.
+
+The formal definitions \path{primeTauShift}, \path{primeTauPhase}, and
+\path{primeTauObservable} use the canonical character \path{ffChar} in
+characteristic $p$.  Their theorem statements cover the identities above for
+arbitrary $p$.  The declarations whose names begin with
+\path{tauObservable} or use \path{phaseSign} instead specialize to
+$p=2$, where $\chi(x)=(-1)^{\operatorname{Tr}(x)}$.  This specialization is
+appropriate only for the subsequent test, whose admissible sizes satisfy
+$q=2^k$; it is not substituted for the general statements.
+
+The proofs can be obtained directly from the displayed matrices.  A shift is a
+permutation matrix, a phase matrix has diagonal entries of modulus one, and a
+tensor product of such matrices is unitary.  Iterating the product identity
+gives $\tau^W(a)^p=I$.  Applying this equality to a nonzero eigenvector gives
+$(\lambda^p-1)v=0$, hence $\lambda^p=1$.  Finally, when
+$v\notin V^\perp$, the map $u\mapsto\chi(u\cdot v)$ is a nontrivial character
+of the finite additive group $V$, so its average vanishes.
+
+\section{Blueprint and formalization}
+The source-general definitions and results are linked from
+\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex}, lines~553--633 and
+649--660. Their Lean declarations are \leanid{primeTauShift},
+\leanid{primeTauPhase}, \leanid{primeTauObservable}, and the accompanying
+product, power, unitarity, spectral, commutation, and cancellation theorems.
+They quantify an arbitrary prime characteristic and use the corresponding
+additive character.
+
+The separately named binary declarations are used by the later QPBT chapters.
+They specialize the same formulas to characteristic two and are not linked as
+implementations of the unrestricted source nodes. Thus the blueprint, the
+general Lean interface, and the paper agree; the binary layer is a consumer
+specialization rather than a restriction of the source statement.
+
+\section{Conclusion}
+There is no mathematical restriction in the source-facing formal statements:
+they retain arbitrary prime characteristic and the corresponding canonical
+character.  The characteristic-two declarations are separate corollaries for
+the QPBT parameter regime.  The remaining work is to prove the general
+identities from the explicit matrices and character orthogonality; it does not
+require changing the binary operator definitions.

+\documentclass[11pt]{article}
+
+\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb}
+\usepackage{xurl}
+\usepackage[hidelinks]{hyperref}
+\setlength{\emergencystretch}{2em}
+
+\input{command}
+
+\title{The Exponent Comparison in the Canonical Pauli Basis Test Bound}
+\author{}
+\date{2026-09-02}
+
+\begin{document}
+\maketitle
+
+\section{At a glance}
+
+\begin{itemize}
+  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Low.  One intermediate inequality in the source
+  does not follow from the canonical parameter definition, but the claimed
+  soundness bound follows by estimating the same term directly.
+  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} The remaining formal argument is an
+  elementary real-analytic estimate of roughly 30--60 lines.
+  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Mathlib supplies inequalities for real
+  powers, exponentials, and logarithms; the project-specific step unfolds the
+  canonical parameters and soundness function.
+  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} The function
+  $(\log R)^{a+b}R^{-b}$ is bounded for $R\geq 4$, and the canonical lower and
+  upper bounds on $m$ transfer this estimate to the third soundness term.
+  Tracked in
+  \href{https://github.com/Dengnifer/MIPStarRE-A/issues/16}{GitHub issue \#16};
+  the parent blueprint task is \localissue{0002}.
+\end{itemize}
+
+\section{Key theorem forms}
+
+Let $a\geq 1$ and $0<b<1$ be the universal constants in the soundness
+function
+\[
+  \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q)
+    = a(md)^a\bigl(\eps^b+q^{-b}+2^{-bmd}\bigr).
+\]
+For $R\geq4$, let $c$ be the least even integer at least $(a+b)/b$, set
+$k=c\lceil\log_2\log_2 R\rceil+1$ and $q=2^k$, and let $j$ be determined by
+$2^j\leq c\lceil\log_2 R\rceil+1<2^{j+1}$. The remaining canonical parameters
+are $m=2^j$ and $d=1$. In particular,
+$m\geq (c/2)\log_2 R\geq\log_2 R$. The required estimate for the third summand is
+\[
+  a m^a 2^{-bm} \leq C'(\log R)^{-b},
+\]
+for a constant $C'$ depending only on $a$ and $b$.  This estimate, together
+with the source bounds for the first two summands, gives the asserted
+polylogarithmic bound for $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}$.
+
+\section{The source comparison}
+
+The canonical parameters are defined in \cite[lines~1503--1514]{Ji2020MIPStar},
+and the bound and its proof occupy lines~1520--1562. At line~1543 the proof
+replaces $2^{-bmd}$ by $q^{-b}$ using the assertion $k\leq m$.%
+\footnote{Tracked in
+\href{https://github.com/Dengnifer/MIPStarRE-A/issues/16}{GitHub issue \#16}.
+The canonical parameter definition is at
+\path{references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex},
+lines~1503--1514; the bound and its proof are at lines~1520--1562, with the
+disputed comparison at line~1543.}
+That comparison does not follow from the stated parameter choice.  For example,
+the allowed values $a=1$ and $b=1/2$ give $c=4$, and $R=5$ gives $k=9$ but
+$m=8$.  Thus the displayed justification is false even though the lemma's
+conclusion remains valid.
+
+The third term can instead be bounded independently of $q$.  Since $d=1$ and
+$m\geq (c/2)\log R\geq\log R$,
+\[
+  2^{-bm}\leq R^{-b}.
+\]
+The accompanying upper bound $m\leq 2c\log R$ therefore gives
+\[
+  a m^a2^{-bm}
+    \leq a(2c)^a(\log R)^aR^{-b}
+    = a(2c)^a\bigl((\log R)^{a+b}R^{-b}\bigr)(\log R)^{-b}.
+\]
+The parenthesized factor is bounded on $R\geq4$: it is continuous and tends
+to zero as $R$ tends to infinity.  Absorbing its supremum into the universal
+constant yields the required estimate.
+
+\section{Comparison with the blueprint and formalization}
+
+The blueprint retains the source statement and uses the direct estimate above.
+The formal theorem has the same hypotheses and conclusion; its docstring marks
+the corrected intermediate argument and cites this note.%
+\footnote{The formal statement is
+\leanid{exists\_deltaQld\_introParams\_bound} in
+\doclink{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Test/CanonicalParams.lean}.}
+
+\section{Conclusion}
+
+The source's comparison $k\leq m$ is false for some permitted constants and
+values of $R$.  It is not needed: the canonical lower bound on $m$ controls the
+third soundness term directly and proves the same final estimate after enlarging
+the universal constant.
+
+\bibliographystyle{alpha}
+\bibliography{references}
+
+\end{document}

+\documentclass[11pt]{article}
+\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb}
+\usepackage{xurl}
+\usepackage[hidelinks]{hyperref}
+\input{command}
+
+\title{Index Pairing in the Low-Degree Sandwich}
+\author{}
+\date{2026-09-03}
+
+\begin{document}
+\maketitle
+
+\section{At a glance}
+\begin{itemize}
+  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Low. The source has a typographical mismatch
+  between a measurement family and the outcome supplied to it.
+  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} The correction changes only the displayed
+  index pairing; the imported proof applies without a new estimate.
+  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} No Mathlib result is needed to identify
+  the mismatch. The formal statement uses a dependent family of outcome types.
+  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Each projector must receive an
+  outcome from its own alphabet, and an empty ordered product equals the
+  identity. The correction is tracked in
+  \href{https://github.com/Dengnifer/MIPStarRE-A/issues/16}{GitHub issue \#16}
+  and descends from \localissue{0002}.
+\end{itemize}
+
+\section{Key theorem forms: the printed statement}
+For $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$, let $G^{i,x}$ be a projective measurement with
+outcome set $\mathcal G_i$. The source prints the sandwich as
+\[
+  G^{k,x}_{g_1}\cdots G^{1,x}_{g_k}\cdots G^{k,x}_{g_1}.
+\]
+This expression is not defined for a general family of outcome sets: the
+outer factor belongs to the measurement indexed by $\mathcal G_k$, whereas
+$g_1$ belongs to $\mathcal G_1$. The mismatch occurs in
+\cite[lines~465--501, especially lines~484--488]{Ji2020MIPStar}.
+
+The result is imported there from Fact~4.34 of the NEEXP paper
+\cite[lines~952--973, especially lines~965--968]{Natarajan2018NEEXP}, mirrored
+at \path{references/neexp-paper/05_quantum_preliminaries.tex}. That statement
+pairs every measurement with its own outcome, giving
+\[
+  G^{k,x}_{g_k}\cdots G^{2,x}_{g_2}G^{1,x}_{g_1}
+  G^{2,x}_{g_2}\cdots G^{k,x}_{g_k}.
+\]
+The order of the operators is unchanged; only the subscripts are corrected.
+
+\section{Blueprint and formalization}
+The blueprint uses the type-correct pairing in
+\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex}, lines~398--425, and explains
+the discrepancy at lines~430--432 in \path{rem:ld-sandwich-indexing}. The formal definition
+\leanid{sandwichProduct} uses an outcome function whose value at $i$ belongs
+to the outcome type of $G^i$. Thus every operator receives the corresponding
+component $g_i$. When $k=0$, the product is empty and its value is the identity,
+which supplies the unique empty-tuple outcome.
+
+\section{Conclusion}
+The reversed outcome subscripts in the source are a typographical error, not a
+different mathematical construction. The blueprint and Lean statement retain
+the source's operator order while restoring the only type-correct pairing.
+
+\bibliographystyle{alpha}
+\bibliography{references}
+\end{document}

    18	
    19	When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
    20	should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
    21	missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
    22	discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
    23	In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same

    27	has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
    28	record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
    29	mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.

    31	The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
    32	cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or

    48	
    49	\section{Concision and Readability}
    50	
    51	A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
    52	in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
    53	uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
    54	checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
    55	\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
    56	formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
    57	implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
    58	and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.
    59	
    60	The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
    61	\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
    62	reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the

    64	and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long

    72	forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
    73	belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.

    75	If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and

    80	\section{When the Investigation Starts}

    82	The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
    83	than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
    84	that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
    85	statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
    86	hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which

    88	argument.
    89	
    90	The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
    91	after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
    92	already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
    93	inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
    94	formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
    95	relevant files already compile.
    96	
    97	At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
    98	local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
    99	intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a

   118	
   119	\section{When to Write a Note}
   120	
   121	A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
   122	match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
   123	estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
   124	conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
   125	identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
   126	probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
   127	a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction

   131	A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a

   153	This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as

We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
properties of the low-degree test.

\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
  \label{def:ld-meas}
  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
  $\F_q$.
  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
\end{definition}

Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.

\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
such that the following
  holds.
  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
  \begin{equation*}
    \begin{split}
      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
			 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}
      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
      G^\bob_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}\;,
    \end{split}
  \end{equation*}
  where $\delta_{\ld} = \delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc)$, 
  and all three statements are with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$.
In addition, the first two approximations hold under the uniform distribution over $u\in \F_q^m$,
	whereas there is no question distribution associated with the third approximation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
and $m$ divides $q$. Let $\Sigma=\F_q$. Let $\code \subseteq \Sigma^q$ be the Reed-Solomon code with degree $d$. Explicitly, $\code$ is the set of all $(p(x_1),\ldots,p(x_n))$ where $p:\F_q\to\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are an enumeration of $\F_q$. Then in the (standard) notation from~\cite{ji2021quantum} $\code$ is a linear $[q,d+1,n-d+1]_\Sigma$ code.

Observe that the two-prover tensor code test, for the code $\code^{\otimes m}$, as described in~\cite[Figure 1 and Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}, is identical to the game $\game^\ld$ with parameters $\ldparams$ and $\ldc=1$, whose decider is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}. This is because 
\begin{enumerate}
\item The \emph{axis-parallel line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{axis-parallel lines test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with the only difference that in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} the roles of A and B are chosen uniformly at random. This is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor code test from~\cite[Section 4.1]{ji2021quantum}.
\item The \emph{diagonal line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{subcube commutation test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with again the added symmetrization between players. 
\item The \emph{consistency test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{synchronicity test} from~\cite[Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}.
\end{enumerate}

As a result,~\cite[Theorem 4.7]{ji2021quantum}, in which we choose the parameter $k$ as $k=m^3d$,  immediately yields \Cref{lem:ld-soundness}.

To conclude it remains to extend the result to the case of general $\ldc$. This is done 
via a standard reduction, following exactly the same steps as the derivation of Theorem 4.43 from Theorem 4.40 in~\cite{NW19}.
\end{proof}






\subsubsection{Complexity of the classical low-degree test.}
The CL functions and decision procedure of the low-degree test are incorporated
as subroutines in some of the normal form verifiers constructed in subsequent
sections.
The next lemma establishes the time complexity of these procedures as a function
of the parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q,m,d,k)$.
The lemma also establishes the time complexity of computing the {description} of
the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ as a Turing machine, given the parameter
tuple $\ldparams$ as input.



\begin{lemma}[Complexity of the classical low-degree test]
  \label{lem:ld-complexity}
  Let $\ldparams = (q,m,d,k)$ denote a parameter tuple.
  \begin{enumerate}
	\item The time complexity of the decision procedure $\decider^\ld$
    parametrized by $\ldparams$ is $\poly(m, d, k, \log q)$.
	\item The time complexity of evaluating marginals of the CL functions
    $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$, and $L_\DLine$ at a given input point is $\poly(m, \log
    q)$.
\begin{remark}[Diagonal questions with zero direction]\label{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}
	The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\ell(u_0, 0) = \{u_0\}$, every $t \in \F_q$ satisfies $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, so any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount; the game-correspondence obligation enumerated in the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} accounts for this event explicitly, and an error of this shape is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.
\end{remark}

The soundness properties of the low individual degree game are expressed in terms of the following class of measurements.

   154	/-- The quantitative error function in `lem:ld-soundness`.  Its argument order
   155	is `(a, b, ε, q, m, d, k)`. -/
   156	noncomputable def deltaLd (a b ε : ℝ) (q m d k : ℕ) : ℝ :=
   157	  a * Real.rpow (((d * m * k : ℕ) : ℝ)) a *
   158	    (Real.rpow ε b + Real.rpow (q : ℝ) (-b) +
   159	      Real.rpow 2 (-(b * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ))))
   160	
   161	/-- Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low individual degree
   162	test (`lem:ld-soundness`, blueprint lines 135--160; paper theorem and proof
   163	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:413-458`).
   164	
   165	The first two consistency bounds compare the point-answer postprocessing of the
   166	strategy with evaluations of the polynomial measurements. Answers of the wrong
   167	form are folded into the zero tuple so that the point family remains a POVM.

   169	The source reduction still requires proofs of the claimed game correspondence
   170	and of the auxiliary parameter bound. These two open facts are detailed in
   171	`docs/paper-gaps/qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility.tex` and
   172	`rem:ld-soundness-provider`, and are tracked by issue #16. -/
   173	theorem exists_ld_soundness :
   174	    ∃ a b : ℝ, 1 ≤ a ∧ 0 < b ∧ b ≤ 1 ∧
   175	      ∀ (L : LdParams) (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε →
   176	        ∀ S : Strategy (ldGame L), S.IsProjective → 1 - ε ≤ S.value →
   177	          ∃ GA : PolyMeasTuple L S.ιA, ∃ GB : PolyMeasTuple L S.ιB,
   178	            consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution (Fin L.m → ScalarQ L))
   179	                (fun u outcome =>
   180	                  heteroKron
   181	                    (((S.A (ldPointQuestionOf L u)).postprocess
   182	                      (ldPointValuesOrZero L)).effect outcome) 1)
   183	                (fun u outcome =>
   184	                  heteroKron 1
   185	                    ((GB.postprocess (evalPolyTupleAt u)).effect outcome))
   186	                S.ψ ≤ deltaLd a b ε L.q L.m L.d L.k ∧
   187	            consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution (Fin L.m → ScalarQ L))
   188	                (fun u outcome =>
   189	                  heteroKron
   190	                    ((GA.postprocess (evalPolyTupleAt u)).effect outcome) 1)
   191	                (fun u outcome =>
   192	                  heteroKron 1
   193	                    (((S.B (ldPointQuestionOf L u)).postprocess
   194	                      (ldPointValuesOrZero L)).effect outcome))
   195	                S.ψ ≤ deltaLd a b ε L.q L.m L.d L.k ∧
   196	            consistencyDefect (uniformDistribution Unit)
   197	                (fun _ g => heteroKron (GA.effect g) 1)
   198	                (fun _ g => heteroKron 1 (GB.effect g))
   199	                S.ψ ≤ deltaLd a b ε L.q L.m L.d L.k := by
   200	  sorry

    10	low-degree component of the Pauli basis test.  The maps are explicit maps on
    11	the ambient coefficient space; their conditional-linearity and distribution
    12	invariants are recorded as proof-level obligations for later stages.
    13	
    14	## References
    15	
    16	The source-facing nodes are `def:ld-game`, `def:ld-question-distribution`, and
    17	`def:ld-win-predicate` in
    18	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`; their paper origin is
    19	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

    30	/-- Numerical parameters for the low-degree game.  The ambient coefficient
    31	space uses the once-and-for-all model `fixedFieldModel P.q P.hq`, rather than a
    32	model supplied by each parameter record.  This is the Lean carrier for
    33	`def:ld-game` in
    34	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`, with paper origin
    35	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    36	-/
    37	structure LdParams where
    38	  q : ℕ
    39	  m : ℕ
    40	  d : ℕ
    41	  k : ℕ
    42	  hm : 1 ≤ m
    43	  hd : 1 ≤ d
    44	  hk : 1 ≤ k
    45	  hq : IsAdmissibleSize q
    46	  hdvd : m ∣ q
    47	
    48	/-- The fixed model accessor for an `LdParams` record.  It is a compatibility
    49	view of the global `fixedFieldModel` selector, not an independently quantified
    50	parameter.  Blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
    51	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    52	-/
    53	noncomputable def LdParams.model (P : LdParams) : FixedFieldModel P.q :=
    54	  fixedFieldModel P.q P.hq
    55	
    56	/-- The scalar carrier selected by an `LdParams` record; this is the fixed
    57	field carrier in `def:ld-game`, selected globally by `LdParams.model`.
    58	Blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`, paper origin
    59	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    60	-/
    61	abbrev ScalarQ (P : LdParams) := (P.model).K
    62	
    63	/-- The three low-degree question types of `def:ld-game`, blueprint
    64	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`, paper origin
    65	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    66	-/
    67	inductive LdType where
    68	  | point
    69	  | aline
    70	  | dline
    71	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    72	
    73	/-- The register index used by the low-degree game (`def:ld-game`, blueprint
    74	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
    75	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
    76	-/
    77	abbrev LdIndex (P : LdParams) := (Fin P.m ⊕ Unit) ⊕ Fin P.m
    78	
    79	/-- The full ambient low-degree coefficient space (`def:ld-game`, blueprint
    80	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
    81	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).

    83	abbrev LdSpace (P : LdParams) := LdIndex P → ScalarQ P

    86	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

    88	def LdSpace.point {P : LdParams} (z : LdSpace P) : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
    89	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl i))
    90

    92	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

    94	def LdSpace.seed {P : LdParams} (z : LdSpace P) : ScalarQ P :=

    97	/-- The direction coordinates of an ambient low-degree vector in
    98	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

   100	def LdSpace.direction {P : LdParams} (z : LdSpace P) : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=

   102	
   103	/-- The integer-coordinate map `χ` from the fixed field representation.  This
   104	is `eq:chi-func` in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
   105	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
   106	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   107	-/
   108	noncomputable def chiIndex (P : LdParams) (s : ScalarQ P) : Fin P.m := by
   109	  letI : NeZero P.m := ⟨by
   110	    exact Nat.ne_of_gt (lt_of_lt_of_le Nat.zero_lt_one P.hm)⟩
   111	  exact Fin.ofNat P.m ((binaryRepresentation P.model s).val / (P.q / P.m))
   112	
   113	/-- The projection used in the diagonal-line map zeroes coordinates before the
   114	chosen index and retains the suffix of the direction vector.  This is the
   115	prefix restriction in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
   116	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
   117	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   118	-/
   119	def prefixProjection {P : LdParams} (i : Fin P.m) (v : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P) :
   120	    Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
   121	  fun j => if j.val < i.val then 0 else v j
   122	
   123	/-- The point CL map, retaining the point block and clearing the auxiliary
   124	blocks.  It is the map `L_point` of `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
   125	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
   126	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   127	-/
   128	def ldPointCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
   129	  fun i => match i with
   130	  | .inl (.inl j) => z (.inl (.inl j))
   131	  | .inl (.inr _) => 0
   132	  | .inr _ => 0
   133	
   134	/-- The affine-line CL map.  The direction block is put through the canonical
   135	line representative map from `def:line-representative`, while the point block
   136	is retained (blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`; paper
   137	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
   138	-/
   139	noncomputable def ldALineCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
   140	  let i := chiIndex P (z.seed)
   141	  let rep := lineRepMap (coordinateDirection i)
   142	  fun i => match i with
   143	  | .inl (.inl j) => (rep (z.point)) j
   144	  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
   145	  | .inr _ => 0
   146	
   147	/-- The diagonal-line CL map, using the same canonical representative interface
   148	for the direction block.  This is the `L_DLine` clause of
   149	`def:ld-question-distribution` (blueprint
   150	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`; paper origin
   151	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
   152	-/
   153	noncomputable def ldDLineCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
   154	  let i := chiIndex P (z.seed)
   155	  let direction := prefixProjection i (z.direction)
   156	  let rep := lineRepMap direction
   157	  fun i => match i with
   158	  | .inl (.inl j) => (rep (z.point)) j
   159	  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
   160	  | .inr j => direction j

   167	noncomputable def ldCL (P : LdParams) : LdType → LdSpace P → LdSpace P

   224	abbrev LdAnswerCode (P : LdParams) :=

   234	noncomputable def ldAnswerEquiv (P : LdParams) :
   235	    LdAnswer P ≃ LdAnswerCode P where

   237	    | .pointVals a => .inl a
   238	    | .alinePolys a => .inr (.inl a)
   239	    | .dlinePolys a => .inr (.inr a)

   241	    | .inl a => .pointVals a
   242	    | .inr (.inl a) => .alinePolys a
   243	    | .inr (.inr a) => .dlinePolys a

   249	    | inr x =>
   250	        cases x with
   251	        | inl a => rfl
   252	        | inr a => rfl
